In 2019 I left Ankober with one suitcase. A few clothes. A few books.
From Lamberet, my friend and I took a taxi and crossed Addis Ababa. He knows the city. I did not know it.
differences: 'he knows the city' (present) becomes 'he knew the city' (past)

meta.literal: We got off at Autobus Tera. It was there that the fear came.
Many people. Much noise. A city filled with light.
Holding my suitcase tightly, I followed him through the crowd, as we looked for a place to stay near the bus station.
In the morning a bus takes me to Bahir Dar, to the university.
differences: Tense changed: the spoken line uses the present/future imperfective ('takes' or 'will take me'), but the subtitle's 'would take me' makes it a past habit or a conditional.

meta.literal: That night sleep did not take me.
If I could speak to that child today, I would tell him this: Don't be afraid. There are many things you will learn in life.
It was around midday when I set out from Ankober. Carrying only one backpack. A friend of mine had come to see me off.
Up to Debre Birhan the road was gravel (unpaved). After that, asphalt.
I was sitting by the window of the bus. Outside is forest and mountain. The view was wonderful.
When I reached Lamberet, it had become evening. My friend was waiting for me. There were many people; building lights, many cars.
When we arrived at Autobus Tera, brokers surrounded us. "Do you want a bed?" They were many. We were confused. We chose one.
The room was a one-bed room. Not very good, and not bad either. It was clean.
In the morning we stood in a long line and bought tickets.
If I met that boy today, I would tell him only one thing: live it.
Two thousand twelve, Year of Mercy. At midday I set out from Ankober. Carrying only one backpack. A friend of mine saw me off.
When I reach Lamberet, it has already become night. My friend is waiting for me right there. People, lights, cars; all at once.
differences: The friend's waiting is in the present tense ('is waiting for me') in the spoken line, but the subtitle puts it in the past ('was there, waiting').

I sat by the window. Outside was only forest and mountain. The view amazed me.
As soon as I finished twelfth grade, I was assigned to Bahir Dar University; right then a new chapter began.
My journey began from Ankober, carrying only one backpack and a mind filled with questions.
First to Debre Birhan, next to Addis Ababa, and finally to Bahir Dar.
As I looked through the window, the road and the landscape kept changing; forest and mountains, valleys and stretching roads.
When I arrived at Autobus Tera it was dusk; my friend met me right there.
People move in every direction, cars pass by, and brokers ask, saying, "Do you want a bed?"
For a moment, it seemed to me that everything was too much all at once and confusing.
In the end we chose a one-bed room; it was not the very best, and it was not bad either, but it was clean enough to rest.
The next morning, to continue the journey, we lined up in a long queue and bought tickets.
When I remember that first night I left home, there is one thing I say to everyone who leaves the familiar world and begins a new journey: the first night is always confusing. Do not flee. Savour it.
I will never forget the first night I spent far from my home. The time was Meskerem 2012.
As soon as I finished twelfth grade, I was assigned to Bahir Dar University. At midday, carrying only one backpack, with my friend seeing me off, I set out from Ankober.
The road was gravel (dirt) as far as Debre Birhan, then it was asphalt.
Sitting by the window, I was watching the forest and the mountain in wonder.
When I arrived at Lamberet after it got dark, another friend of mine was waiting for me. Addis Ababa received me flooded with people, lights and cars; I lost track of where to look.
And when we reached Autobus Tera, brokers surrounded us.
"Do you want a bed? A bed?" We were confused about whom to listen to. In the end we followed one of them.
The room was a single-bed room; it was neither good nor bad; but it was clean.
The next morning, having lined up in a long queue, we bought a ticket for Bahir Dar.
Today, seven years later, I have one thing I say to everyone who leaves home: the first night is always confusing. But the confusion is part of the journey. Do not flee from it; savour it.
